articles.text: The Dominion government is making concessions to Riel.
articles.summary: Note that the Canadian government is making concessions to Louis Riel.

articles.text: The order of President Arthur, opening the Winnebago reservation has been rescined by President Cleveland. There is great injustice in this to the settlers as many will be hopelessly bankrupted. Troops will be necessary to expel the settlers. Indignation meetings are being held and well they may be, as the Indians do not need or even want the land now occupied by settlers.
articles.summary: Editorial objecting to President Cleveland's rescinding of Arthur's order opening the Winnebago reservation to settlers.

articles.text: As will be seen in another article, a strong feeling seems to have grown up against stock interests among the numerous farming class. It is difficult to give a reason for this feeling except on the ground of envy. Almost invariably a stock country is in no sense an agricultural country and vice versa. Consequently their interests do not clash but on the other hand are in many ways dependent on and an aid to each other. We ask our brothers of the eastern press to examine the facts carefully before condemning unheard the principal industry of the west.
articles.summary: Editorial arguing that farming and stock interests do not clash and asking the eastern press not to condemn the cattle industry.

articles.text: There seems to be scarcely a doubt that England and Russia will go to war. Both are defiant and neither cares in the least to explain any of its actions to the other. Both have repeatedly knocked chips off the other's shoulder and as Russia has stepped over England's line, England is now shedding her coat preparatory to "give a licking, take a licking, lick or be licked." As to which wins, makes little difference to the United States. If they will only stop their quarrelling and go to fighting, it will make our beef and wheat men the happiest set in existence. Sic 'em, Bull, sic 'em Bear.
articles.summary: Editorial predicting war between England and Russia, which would benefit American beef and wheat producers.

articles.text: Strange as it may seem, Gen. Grant is constantly improving. There is a very well defined suspicion that the physicians did not diagnose his case correctly and that the national patient is not really suffering from cancer. Be this as it may, Gen. Grant's sickness and near approach to death have shown conclusively the place he occupied in the hearts of his countrymen. There is no other citizen of the United States, whose health would have been so closely watched. No other citizen whose death would have been so sincerely mourned. Gen. Grant is to-day the foremost citizen of the United States.
articles.summary: Editorial on Gen. U. S. Grant's improving health and his place in the nation's affection.

articles.text: As we stated once before, we are in a position to know whereof we speak, when we state that ere now a railroad would have been built from Medora to the Hills or a good share of the distance, had the Hills merchants stuck to their written and spoken pledges to ship via the Northern Pacific. The writen contracts were handed to capitalists who were ready to build as soon as it was proved that these merchants would ship as much as estimated. The estimate was low and if all the merchants had done as they agreed, twice the estimated amount of freight, would have been shipped and the Hills people would now have direct or easy railroad connections. As it was, not half nor a quarter of the merchants stood to their agreements and less than that proportion of the freight came by the way of the N. P. It did not make a particle of difference at what point the goods were forwarded, so long as they were sent over the Northern Pacific. This freight was the only guide the capitalists had to go by in figuring on the road and it will be only with the greatest difficulty that they can be induced to invest when the facts speak for themselves that the Hills do not have enough freight to pay for a railroad or that Hills merchants do not stick to their bargains. It is a choice of evils, the latter being the solution.
articles.summary: Editorial blaming Black Hills merchants' failure to ship via the Northern Pacific for the lack of a railroad from Medora to the Hills.

articles.text: There are some sayings which are so common that people do not realize their force. Just as spring poets, St. Louis girls' feet and fifty other topics have become butts for the wit of paragraphers, so have cattle companies come to be objects of attack when granger papers want "filling." We are now sorry to see the Bismarck Tribune fall into line with the statement that: "There is one thing for which secretary Lamar ought to be commended by the people of the entire country, and that is the determination to keep cattle kings out of the Indian territory." A sufficient answer to this unsupported statement is, "Why?" We care not how prejudiced the man is, if he honestly attempts to thoroughly answer this question, he will as certainly take the side of the cattlemen as they will their own. The facts are simply these. The part of the Indian Territory in which stockmen now are was a practical desert, of no use to the Indians and not wanted by them. The government had given the Territory to the Indians, however, and only by their consent could cowmen move in. This consent was gained and offers were then immediately made to buy or lease from the government also, so as to get as good a title as possible. Repeatedly have the cowmen tried this but the government has invariably refused payment, although tacitly acknowledging the right of the Indians to lease by leaving the stockmen in undisturbed possession. Even as late as April 7th the cowmen tried earnestly to induce the government to lease to them and they stand willing at any time to pay a fair rental. No one is disturbed by the presence of cattle in the Indian territory, the Indians are satisfied and again we ask: "Why should secretary Lamar be commended."
articles.summary: Editorial rebutting the Bismarck Tribune's praise of Secretary Lamar for keeping cattlemen out of Indian Territory.

articles.headline: STOCK NOTES. Strayed or Stolen.
articles.text: From Little Missouri, July 6, 1884, a bay horse, eight years old and weighing about 1,000 pounds. The horse was branded with an anchor on left cheek and a hat brand on left shoulder. On the left hip he had a Texas brand, looking something like 7N, connected with flourish at top of N. A reward of $25 will be paid for information leading to his recovery. The horse is the property of John Pohl, and information can be brought or sent to the Cow Boy office.
articles.summary: Notice of a bay horse belonging to John Pohl strayed or stolen from Little Missouri on July 6, 1884; $25 reward.

articles.text: Large horses of all kinds are higher now than they have been for twenty years. There is no danger of the supply outgrowing the demand, as there is always a ready market for good large horses.
articles.summary: Prices for large horses are the highest in twenty years.

articles.text: We are in receipt of a letter from Russ Wilson, foreman of the E 6 in which he states that the horses are looking first-rate, being fat and lively. The grass is well up and looks like the map of Ireland, the cattle are looking well and there is a prospect of a large calf-crop. Preparations are nearly completed for the round-up and everyone is busy.
articles.summary: Russ Wilson, foreman of the E 6 outfit, reports stock in fine condition and round-up preparations nearly complete.

articles.text: The Wyoming association at their last meeting appointed a committee to see about getting passes for its members. The committee, with John N. Simpson at its head, met a committee representing the lines in question and the subject was put off until the official meeting of the lines.
articles.summary: The Wyoming stock association's committee on railroad passes, headed by John N. Simpson, was put off.

articles.text: We commend the New Mexico Stock Grower for the firm stand it has taken against the reckless shooting sometimes practiced by cowboys. It has utterly lost any power even of amusement to outsiders. The Stock Grower says: "This 'bad-man-with-a-gun' business is foolish, cowardly and unmanly and will be stopped in the near future, and some of the experts at 'shooting up things' will find themselves rustling for jobs with none in sight."
articles.summary: Endorses the New Mexico Stock Grower's stand against reckless shooting by cowboys.

articles.text: That contagious pleuro-pneumonia has really broken out near Fulton, Mo., there seems no reason to doubt. Gov. Marmaduke. all the stockmen of Missouri and commissionor Coleman are taking active measures to stamp out the disease and as everyone is working to that end it is believed that it will not spread at all. Only heroic measurs will be successful. It is absolutely necessary to kill every animal that has the disease and put those that have been exposed, under the strictest quarantine. Already about two hundred animals have been killed and others will be at the first symptom of the disease.
articles.summary: Outbreak of contagious pleuro-pneumonia near Fulton, Missouri, and measures to stamp it out.

articles.text: Norman J. Coleman, commissioner of Agriculture has asked the following open questions of the cowmen of fifty-nine Texas counties, with a view to securing a modification of the quarantine enactment and a relief to the present depressed state of the Texas cattle industry: "1. Have you purchased any bulls or other cattle, or do you know of any that have been bought from north of the south line of Kansas to your vicinity, or to any part of any of the counties named above? If so, state the number, the location as near as possible to which they were taken, and the number, if any, which died of acclimatization fever. 2. Do you know of any case in which cattle from the eastern counties of Texas have been taken to the counties above named in the spring or summer months, and allowed to pasture on the same ranges with the cattle native to these counties. If so, state if any disease occurred among the native cattle, and give symptoms and numbers afflicted as far as possible."
articles.summary: Commissioner of Agriculture Norman J. Coleman's questions to Texas cowmen on quarantine and Texas fever.

articles.text: The Kansas City Journal tells of a game of poker played recently in that city between Major Drumm and a Texan. The Journal says the Texan had no money but plenty of cattle and an immense desire to play poker with the major. The latter is known around the stock-yards for his great natural resources, and he swept away the seemingly insurmountable difficulty by proposing a game of one steer ante, two steers to come and no limit. They played on this basis. Major Drumm dealt and the gentleman from Texas antied one steer. Both came in and the game opened with four steers on the table. Major Drumm drew two tens and caught an unexpected full, while the gentleman from Texas struck a bobtail snag and passed out. The third was a jack pot and it took three deals to open it. The gentleman from Texas finally drew two jacks and opened the pot with a fine breeding bull, which counted six. Major Drumm covered this with five steers and a two-year-old heifer, and went him twelve better. The gentleman from Texas who drew another jack saw the twelve cows and went fifty steers, twenty two-year-old heifers, four bulls and twenty-five heifers better. Major Drumm looked at his hand and placed upon the table six fine Alderney cows, five imported Durham bulls, one hundred grass fed two-year-olds, fifty prime to medium corn-fed Colorado half-breed steers, with a side bet of a Normandy gelding to cover the bar bill. The man from Texas made his bet good with an even two hundred and fifty straight Kansas wintered Texas half-breeds and ten Scotch polled cattle, fourteen mustangs and the ne 1/4 of the sw 1/4 of section 10 of the Panhandle of Texas, and called. Major Drumm held three aces, and put in his hip pocket 750 steers, heifers, etc, and a big stock ranch.
articles.summary: Humorous Kansas City Journal story of a poker game played for cattle between Major Drumm and a Texan.

articles.text: A number of sales of Texas cattle have lately been made at fair prices, in Texas. They are mostly stock cattle and will go to fill ranges depleted by last summer's sales and this winter's losses.
articles.summary: Recent sales of Texas stock cattle at fair prices.

articles.text: Some action should be taken by our cowmen to prevent round-ups after the beef round-up in the fall. This is the time when the cattle become attached to one range and, if not disturbed are liable to remain there all winter, only drifting back and forth a little way to avoid storms. If they are disturbed and driven off their range they are liable to drift hundreds of miles. If this subject is discussed in time it will save many dollars to our cowmen.
articles.summary: Urges local cowmen to stop round-ups after the fall beef round-up so cattle stay on their ranges.

articles.headline: ROUND-UP DISTRICTS
articles.text:
Below are the three round-up districts in which our cowmen are interested. They will be kept standing until they begin. It will be noticed that the Powder river round-up begins May 7 and the Yellowstone and Little Missouri begin May 25.

ROUND-UP DISTRCT No. 5.

Beginning at the mouth of Powder river, May 7, 1885; thence working down the Yellowstone river on the south side to the mouth of O'Fallon creek; thence up O'Fallon creek and its tributaries to its head; thence across to the head of Little Beaver; thence down Little Beaver to within ten miles of its mouth: thence across to the head of Big Beaver; thence down Big Beaver to the Northern Pacific railroad; thence across to the head of Glendive creek and down to the Yellowstone river; thence up the Yellowstone river including Cedar creek to the mouth of Cabin creek; thence up Cabin creek to its head. J. H. Lander, foreman.

ROUND-UP DISTRICT No. 6.

Beginning at the mouth of Box Elder, May 25, 1885; thence working down the Little Missouri and its tributaries to a point about twenty miles below the mouth of Big Beaver; thence up Big Beaver and its tributaries to the Northern Pacific railroad. W. P. Osterhout, foreman.

ROUND-UP DISTRICT No. 7.

Beginning May 25, 1885, at the mouth of the Yellowstone river, thence working up the Yellowstone river and tributaries on the east side to Glendive and the Northern Pacific railroad. R. H. Moore, foreman.
articles.summary: Routes, start dates and foremen of round-up districts 5, 6 and 7 for 1885.

articles.text: The cowboy seems to be losing the pristine gorgeousness of his character. Only a few years ago people knew him as a wild and terrible factor in the development of the west. He had things his own way, took possession of towns, ran whole counties, and if he did not drink hot blood, shed it with a recklessness that painted all the streams that sloped away from the Rockies a delicious pinky red. He was the ideal b-a-a-d man from the head-waters of Bitter creek. He ate fire and spat snow. He was wild and wooly and hard to carry. When he ordered a drink it was rattle-snakes' stings with the bite in them. When he sat down to a restaurant table it was to demand a white man's liver and a dead nigger's toe-nales. He waded in gore, and was always in the business of starting graveyards in new towns where the locality was too healthy for any other kind of sudden death than that which comes with old age. This is only a feeble suggestion of what the old-time cowboy of fiction was. In his most peaceful moments he had his hand on his revolver and a big bowie knife between his teeth. His word was law. The statutes of the United States had no more weight than his simple say so. He carried his own court with him, and when the time came to pronounce sentence, whether he was right or wrong, this ancient cowpuncher seldom failed to administer justice with his six-shooter. Where is such a man?—[St. Louis Globe-Democrat.
articles.summary: Reprinted St. Louis Globe-Democrat sketch lampooning the fictional wild cowboy (contains a period racial slur).

articles.headline: A COWBOY'S PRIMER.
articles.text:
Papa, who is that man?

My child, that is a cowboy.

Why is he standing there?

He is rolling a cigarette, my child.

What is that just over the hill?

That, my child, is a big herd of cattle.

Why is not the cowboy along with the rest?

My darling, his health requires that he must stop for ten minutes and roll a cigarette before leaving camp.

Is his health poor, papa?

Very poor, my child.

See papa, now he is going.

No, my dear; his saddle is not on straight and he has to put it on again.

Ah! look papa, now he is going.

Yes, my child, he is going—to roll another cigarette.

See, he is looking for something

Yes, he is looking for a match.

Will he find his match?

My child, there are no snails in the country.

Does he not see the cattle running.

No, darling.

Oh! but papa, see he has picked up a coal to light his cigarette and it has burned his hand. And look! his horse has ran away.

Yes, my child; when the foreman comes back to camp he will tell him that his horse ran away and in trying to stop him the rope burned his hand.

But papa, that will be a story.

Yes, my dear, two stories and a basement.

Will such a bad cowboy live in such a high house?

Yes, darling; there is a higher place for him.

Where?

In heaven, my child.

We should elongate our features.

—[Dum Colly Oddle.
articles.summary: Humorous catechism mocking the idle cowboy, signed "Dum Colly Oddle."

articles.text: Duck and geese are plentiful up and down the river.
articles.summary: Ducks and geese plentiful along the river.

articles.text: Charlie Jolly is nearly recovered from his recent injury.
articles.summary: Charlie Jolly is recovering from an injury.

articles.text: F. W. McKinney, of Bismarck, stopped over a train Tuesday.
articles.summary: F. W. McKinney of Bismarck visited.

articles.text: McKenzie & O'Brien will soon move their blacksmith shop to this side of the track.
articles.summary: McKenzie & O'Brien will move their blacksmith shop across the track.

articles.text: Dan McKenzie returned Monday evening from a three months' trip to Nova Scotia.
articles.summary: Dan McKenzie returned from three months in Nova Scotia.

articles.text: The stock-yards are completed but are scarcely large enough to receive three car-loads of cattle.
articles.summary: Medora stock-yards are finished but small.

articles.text: Dr. Hebar Robart, of Dickinson, came up last night to see Mrs. Draper who has been ill for some time.
articles.summary: Dr. Hebar Robart of Dickinson came to attend Mrs. Draper.

articles.text: Again were the remaining shoots of the delinquent contestants put off on account of the rain Saturday.
articles.summary: Remaining shooting-contest rounds postponed by rain.

articles.text: Tom Matthews stopped off a train Monday. He has been appointed inspector by the Montana board of stock commissioners.
articles.summary: Tom Matthews, newly appointed Montana stock inspector, stopped at Medora.

articles.text: Those who have been shooting in the rink for prizes must have their scores completed by May 1, as the prizes are given on that day.
articles.summary: Rink shooting scores must be completed by May 1, when prizes are awarded.

articles.text: Jack Bullion's brother, Robert, from Maryland Junction, Minn., has been here several days. He intends putting in some horses with Jack.
articles.summary: Robert Bullion visiting his brother Jack; plans to put in horses with him.

articles.text: Large corralls have been built both here and on Sully creek, in addition to the others the Co. has, to accommodate the cattle here this summer.
articles.summary: The company has built large new corrals at Medora and on Sully creek.

articles.text: "It almost breaks my heart to be the bearer of this sad news. Would that I could suffer for you." Ask the night teleg. to diagram this "goak."
articles.summary: A joke aimed at the night telegraph operator.

articles.text: It is entirely feasible to bore an artesian well here and the water will be entirely free from alkali. We will have something more to say about this matter soon.
articles.summary: The paper says an alkali-free artesian well could be bored at Medora.

articles.text: Word has been received from the Willard Bros., that they will be here Saturday or Sunday, with several car-loads of horses. Several sales have been missed by their delay in coming.
articles.summary: The Willard Bros. are expected with several car-loads of horses.

articles.text: W. H. McKanlass, the colored skater and musician will give an exhibition at the rink to-morrow evening, which promises to be a very interesting entertainment. His performance is highly spoken of by the papers along the line.
articles.summary: Skater and musician W. H. McKanlass to perform at the rink.

articles.text: J. C. Fisher has already set a good example which we hope to see followed extensively, Arbor day, the 25th. Several have already made up their minds to set out trees, which will do much toward improving the looks of our town.
articles.summary: Townspeople plan to plant trees on Arbor Day, April 25, following J. C. Fisher's example.

articles.text: Miss Lou Eleson, of Glendive, will be here Tuesday and Wednesday the 28th and 29th., with a complete assortment of ladies' millinery and fancy goods. Anything desired in this line will be on sale and it will be an excellent opportunity to buy.
articles.summary: Miss Lou Eleson of Glendive will sell millinery in Medora April 28-29.

articles.text: A meeting will be held next Monday evening at the rink to organize a bucket brigade. The movement is a commendable one and it behooves all our citizens to turn out to the meeting. We are liable at any time to have a fire and effectual work can be done with buckets.
articles.summary: Meeting called to organize a bucket brigade for fire protection.

articles.text: To-night at the rink there will be a tournament, the person securing the greatest number of rings to be given a prize. Saturday evening May 2, there will be a masquerade, many of the participants in the last one desiring a repetition. Admission to both entertainments will be only the usual rates.
articles.summary: Ring tournament at the rink tonight and a masquerade May 2.

articles.text: The post-office has been again moved to its old location in the Co's store. The change will not be popular, as lock and call boxes possess many advantages over the general delivery system. It is also rather severe on Mr. Fisher, "wich wuz P. M.," as he had gone to considerable expense in fitting up the office in the rink.
articles.summary: The post-office moved back to the company store from the rink, displacing J. C. Fisher as postmaster.

articles.text: The round-up east of the river and north of the track and to include the whole Killdeer Mt. country will begin May 1. This round-up is for the purpose of driving all the cattle possible to the river so as to be caught in our general round-up. The date for a corresponding round-up south of the track has not been decided.
articles.summary: A preliminary round-up east of the river and north of the track, including the Killdeer Mountain country, begins May 1.

articles.text: We notice in the St. Paul dispatches that day before yesterday a number of prominent cowmen were contracting with the N. P. for the delivery of 40,000 cattle to Medora from Washington territory. On account of the large number of cattle and the fact that several of the cowmen mentioned have all their herds in Montana, we are inclined to discredit the report.
articles.summary: Paper doubts a St. Paul report of a contract to ship 40,000 cattle from Washington Territory to Medora.

articles.text: The rainy, drizzly, snowy weather of Saturday, Sunday, Monday and Tuesday, was a perfect godsend to western Dakota. The rain came scarcely faster than need be to have every drop soak into the ground and this, followed by the damp snow of Tuesday and melted by yesterday's genial weather will fill the ground as full as it can hold of water. One can almost see the grass grow now.
articles.summary: Four days of rain and snow soaked the ground, welcomed as a godsend for the range.

articles.text: Lee Eisenberg, of Bismarck, was here Saturday with a line of dry goods.
articles.summary: Bismarck salesman Lee Eisenberg visited with dry goods.

articles.text: Arthur Smith has almost recovered from his accident of two weeks ago.
articles.summary: Arthur Smith recovering from an accident.

articles.text: Geo. Porter returned from Chicago last Friday night. His wife will return in about ten days.
articles.summary: George Porter returned from Chicago.

articles.text: Theodore Roosevelt came in last Friday night and started almost immediatily for his Elkhorn ranch down the river.
articles.summary: Theodore Roosevelt arrived and left at once for the Elkhorn ranch.

articles.text: Wal. Osterhout went to Miles, Sunday evening to arrange for some horses for Howard Faton, who went up Monday night.
articles.summary: Wal. Osterhout went to Miles City to arrange horses for Howard "Faton" (likely Eaton).

articles.text: "Sadie" Houk, who will be remembered as a Cow Boy comp. last summer passed through Saturday night on his way to Glendive.
articles.summary: Former Cow Boy compositor "Sadie" Houk passed through to Glendive.

articles.text: J. D. Garver returned from Bismarck last Friday, with his family. His wife's health is improved though she is far from well. His sister-in-law also accompanied him.
articles.summary: J. D. Garver returned from Bismarck with his family.

articles.text: If by any chance a subscriber should not get his paper, it would be a favor if the fact were immediately reported to this office. We will rectify any mistake of this nature.
articles.summary: Asks subscribers to report undelivered papers.

articles.text: The body of Mrs. Hawkins, of Spearfish, President Garfield's niece, was brought up on the coach Saturday night from Spearfish and shipped to Mrs. Garfield at Cleveland, Ohio.
articles.summary: Body of Mrs. Hawkins, President Garfield's niece, came through on the stage to be shipped to Cleveland.

articles.text: B. F. Matthias, formerly superintendent of this division of the N. P. is president of the Charlotte Harbor and Northern Central R. R. with headquarters at Tampa, Florida.
articles.summary: Former N. P. division superintendent B. F. Matthias heads a Florida railroad.

articles.text: Mr. T. Martin will make a complete digest of his weather reports for the last six months, to be published in connection with his monthly reports. It will make a valuable paper for reference.
articles.summary: T. Martin will publish a six-month digest of his weather reports.

articles.text: "Skinny" Wallace, who drives on the stage line from Buffalo creek to Middle Grand river, was in town Saturday. While here he laid in a good supply of paint and spread a thin coat over the suburbs.
articles.summary: Stage driver "Skinny" Wallace was in town on a spree.

articles.text: Rev. H. B. Schaffner preached an eloquent sermon in the rink last Sunday evening to a small congregetion. The weather was very stormy which doubtless accounts for the few in attendance. Service will be held every Sunday evening hereafter, at half-past seven.
articles.summary: Rev. H. B. Schaffner preached at the rink; Sunday evening services to continue.

articles.text: Lloyd Roberts returned from Glendive Monday morning and started for St. Cloud again Tuesday morning. He delivered several hundred cattle in Glendive in prime condition. He has also delivered mixed herds in Jamestown and Bismarck. He will return again about May 10.
articles.summary: Lloyd Roberts delivered cattle at Glendive, Jamestown and Bismarck and left for St. Cloud.

articles.text: Our thanks are due A. McCall of the Black Hills for a complete list of house and council bills passed at the last session of the legislature. Mr. McCall originated and with the able assistance of the other Hills members, had the bill passed repealing the herd law and establishing the fence law in the western tier of counties.
articles.summary: Thanks to legislator A. McCall, author of the bill repealing the herd law and establishing the fence law in the western counties.

articles.text: Mr. and Mrs. and Miss Hattie Eaton parents and sister of the Eaton boys, came in Monday evening and for the summer will make their headquarters at the logging camp. Mr. Eaton reported that while we were having splendid weather here, they were having the worst weather in the east, that he ever experienced. For a time it almost paralyzed business.
articles.summary: The Eaton brothers' parents and sister Hattie arrived to spend the summer at the logging camp.

articles.text: Last Friday evening, No. 1 was delayed seven or eight hours by the falling of a huge rock upon the track just east of Sully Springs. A serious accident nearly resulted, as the train could not be stopped until the engine had struck the rock and threw the two front drivers off the track. The rock should have been blasted off long ago as it has been threatening to fall for two or three years.
articles.summary: Westbound No. 1 struck a fallen rock near Sully Springs and was delayed seven or eight hours.

events.date_basis: Undated editorial in Thu 23 Apr 1885 issue; defaulted to the preceding week
events.title: Cow Boy protests Cleveland's closing of the Winnebago reservation
events.summary: The Cow Boy reported that President Cleveland had rescinded President Arthur's order opening the Winnebago reservation, that indignation meetings were being held, and argued settlers would be bankrupted.
events.excerpt: Troops will be necessary to expel the settlers. Indignation meetings are being held and well they may be

events.date_basis: Undated editorial in Thu 23 Apr 1885 issue; defaulted to the preceding week
events.title: Cow Boy blames Black Hills merchants for stalled Medora–Hills railroad
events.summary: The Cow Boy wrote that a railroad from Medora to the Black Hills would already have been built had Hills merchants kept their pledges to ship freight via the Northern Pacific, and that capitalists would now be hard to persuade.
events.excerpt: ere now a railroad would have been built from Medora to the Hills or a good share of the distance, had the Hills merchants stuck to their written and spoken pledges

events.date_basis: Undated editorial in Thu 23 Apr 1885 issue; defaulted to the preceding week
events.title: Cow Boy rebuts Bismarck Tribune over cattlemen in Indian Territory
events.summary: The Cow Boy took issue with the Bismarck Tribune's praise of Secretary Lamar for keeping "cattle kings" out of Indian Territory, arguing the cowmen had Indian consent and had repeatedly offered to lease.
events.excerpt: We are now sorry to see the Bismarck Tribune fall into line

events.date_basis: Dated in notice: "From Little Missouri, July 6, 1884"
events.title: John Pohl's bay horse strayed or stolen from Little Missouri
events.summary: A notice offered a $25 reward for a bay horse belonging to John Pohl, branded with an anchor and a hat brand, that strayed or was stolen from Little Missouri.
events.excerpt: From Little Missouri, July 6, 1884, a bay horse, eight years old and weighing about 1,000 pounds.

events.date_basis: Letter received; undated, defaulted to week before Thu 23 Apr 1885
events.title: E 6 foreman Russ Wilson reports good range conditions
events.summary: The Cow Boy reported a letter from Russ Wilson, foreman of the E 6, saying horses and cattle looked well, the grass was up, and round-up preparations were nearly complete.
events.excerpt: The grass is well up and looks like the map of Ireland, the cattle are looking well and there is a prospect of a large calf-crop.

events.date_basis: Round-up District No. 6 "Beginning at the mouth of Box Elder, May 25, 1885"
events.title: Little Missouri round-up (District No. 6) set to begin May 25
events.summary: The Cow Boy published the 1885 route for Round-up District No. 6, beginning at the mouth of Box Elder creek and working down the Little Missouri, with W. P. Osterhout as foreman.
events.excerpt: Beginning at the mouth of Box Elder, May 25, 1885; thence working down the Little Missouri and its tributaries

events.date_basis: District No. 5 "Beginning at the mouth of Powder river, May 7, 1885"; District No. 7 begins May 25
events.title: Powder River and Yellowstone round-ups (Districts 5 and 7) scheduled
events.summary: The Cow Boy published the 1885 routes for Round-up District No. 5, beginning May 7 at the mouth of Powder River under J. H. Lander, and District No. 7, beginning May 25 at the mouth of the Yellowstone under R. H. Moore.
events.excerpt: the Powder river round-up begins May 7 and the Yellowstone and Little Missouri begin May 25

events.date_basis: Undated item; defaulted to week before Thu 23 Apr 1885
events.title: Ducks and geese plentiful on the Little Missouri
events.summary: The Cow Boy reported ducks and geese plentiful up and down the river.
events.excerpt: Duck and geese are plentiful up and down the river.

events.date_basis: Undated item; defaulted to week before Thu 23 Apr 1885
events.title: Charlie Jolly nearly recovered from injury
events.summary: Charlie Jolly was reported nearly recovered from his recent injury.
events.excerpt: Charlie Jolly is nearly recovered from his recent injury.

events.title: F. W. McKinney of Bismarck stops over at Medora
events.summary: F. W. McKinney of Bismarck stopped over a train at Medora.
events.excerpt: F. W. McKinney, of Bismarck, stopped over a train Tuesday.

events.date_basis: "will soon move" as of Thu 23 Apr 1885
events.title: McKenzie & O'Brien to move blacksmith shop across the track
events.summary: The Cow Boy reported that McKenzie & O'Brien would soon move their blacksmith shop to the Medora side of the track.
events.excerpt: McKenzie & O'Brien will soon move their blacksmith shop to this side of the track.

events.title: Dan McKenzie returns from Nova Scotia
events.summary: Dan McKenzie returned to Medora from a three months' trip to Nova Scotia.
events.excerpt: Dan McKenzie returned Monday evening from a three months' trip to Nova Scotia.

events.date_basis: Undated item; defaulted to week before Thu 23 Apr 1885
events.title: Medora stock-yards completed
events.summary: The Cow Boy reported the stock-yards completed, though scarcely large enough to receive three car-loads of cattle.
events.excerpt: The stock-yards are completed but are scarcely large enough to receive three car-loads of cattle.

events.title: Dickinson doctor called to attend Mrs. Draper
events.summary: Dr. Hebar Robart of Dickinson came up to Medora to see Mrs. Draper, who had been ill for some time.
events.excerpt: Dr. Hebar Robart, of Dickinson, came up last night to see Mrs. Draper who has been ill for some time.

events.title: Rain postpones remaining shooting contest rounds
events.summary: The remaining shoots of delinquent contestants in the rink shooting contest were again put off because of rain.
events.excerpt: Again were the remaining shoots of the delinquent contestants put off on account of the rain Saturday.

events.title: Tom Matthews, new Montana stock inspector, stops at Medora
events.summary: Tom Matthews stopped off a train at Medora; he had been appointed inspector by the Montana board of stock commissioners.
events.excerpt: He has been appointed inspector by the Montana board of stock commissioners.

events.title: Rink shooting prizes to be awarded May 1
events.summary: Contestants shooting for prizes at the rink were told to complete their scores by May 1, when the prizes would be given.
events.excerpt: the prizes are given on that day

events.date_basis: "has been here several days" as of Thu 23 Apr 1885
events.title: Robert Bullion visits brother Jack, plans horse venture
events.summary: Robert Bullion of Maryland Junction, Minn., had been in Medora several days visiting his brother Jack and intended to put in some horses with him.
events.excerpt: He intends putting in some horses with Jack.

events.date_basis: Undated item; defaulted to week before Thu 23 Apr 1885
events.title: New corrals built at Medora and on Sully Creek
events.summary: Large corrals were built at Medora and on Sully Creek, in addition to the company's others, to handle cattle that summer.
events.excerpt: Large corralls have been built both here and on Sully creek

events.date_basis: Undated item; defaulted to week before Thu 23 Apr 1885
events.title: Cow Boy says an artesian well is feasible at Medora
events.summary: The Cow Boy stated it was entirely feasible to bore an artesian well at Medora with water free from alkali.
events.excerpt: It is entirely feasible to bore an artesian well here and the water will be entirely free from alkali.

events.title: Willard Bros. expected with car-loads of horses
events.summary: Word was received that the Willard Bros. would arrive Saturday or Sunday with several car-loads of horses.
events.excerpt: they will be here Saturday or Sunday, with several car-loads of horses

events.title: Skater W. H. McKanlass to give exhibition at the rink
events.summary: W. H. McKanlass, described as a colored skater and musician, was to give an exhibition at the Medora rink.
events.excerpt: will give an exhibition at the rink to-morrow evening

events.title: Medora residents plan Arbor Day tree planting
events.summary: Following J. C. Fisher's example, several residents planned to set out trees on Arbor Day, April 25, to improve the town's looks.
events.excerpt: Several have already made up their minds to set out trees

events.title: Glendive milliner to sell goods in Medora
events.summary: Miss Lou Eleson of Glendive was to be in Medora with ladies' millinery and fancy goods for sale.
events.excerpt: with a complete assortment of ladies' millinery and fancy goods

events.title: Meeting called to organize Medora bucket brigade
events.summary: A meeting was called at the rink to organize a bucket brigade for fighting fires in Medora.
events.excerpt: A meeting will be held next Monday evening at the rink to organize a bucket brigade.

events.title: Ring tournament at the Medora rink
events.summary: A ring tournament was scheduled at the rink, with a prize for whoever secured the most rings.
events.excerpt: To-night at the rink there will be a tournament

events.title: Masquerade planned at the Medora rink
events.summary: A masquerade was planned at the rink, many participants in the last one having asked for a repetition.
events.excerpt: Saturday evening May 2, there will be a masquerade

events.date_basis: Undated item; defaulted to week before Thu 23 Apr 1885
events.title: Medora post-office moved back to the company store
events.summary: The post-office was moved back to its old location in the company's store; the paper said Mr. Fisher, the former postmaster, had spent considerably fitting up the office in the rink.
events.excerpt: The post-office has been again moved to its old location in the Co's store.

events.title: Killdeer Mountain round-up east of the river to begin May 1
events.summary: A round-up east of the Little Missouri and north of the railroad, covering the Killdeer Mountain country, was set for May 1 to drive cattle to the river ahead of the general round-up.
events.excerpt: will begin May 1. This round-up is for the purpose of driving all the cattle possible to the river

events.date_basis: "day before yesterday" relative to undated St. Paul dispatches; within week before Thu 23 Apr 1885
events.title: Cow Boy doubts report of 40,000 cattle to be shipped to Medora
events.summary: St. Paul dispatches reported cowmen contracting with the Northern Pacific to deliver 40,000 cattle to Medora from Washington Territory; the Cow Boy was inclined to discredit the report.
events.excerpt: contracting with the N. P. for the delivery of 40,000 cattle to Medora from Washington territory

events.date_basis: "Saturday, Sunday, Monday and Tuesday" before Thu 23 Apr 1885; "yesterday" = 22 Apr
events.title: Four days of rain and snow soak western Dakota
events.summary: Rainy, drizzly and snowy weather from Saturday through Tuesday, ending with damp snow melted by Wednesday's mild weather, was welcomed as a godsend for western Dakota.
events.excerpt: The rainy, drizzly, snowy weather of Saturday, Sunday, Monday and Tuesday, was a perfect godsend to western Dakota.

events.title: Lee Eisenberg of Bismarck in Medora with dry goods
events.summary: Lee Eisenberg of Bismarck was in Medora with a line of dry goods.
events.excerpt: Lee Eisenberg, of Bismarck, was here Saturday with a line of dry goods.

events.date_basis: Accident "two weeks ago" before Thu 23 Apr 1885
events.title: Arthur Smith recovering from accident
events.summary: Arthur Smith was reported almost recovered from an accident two weeks earlier.
events.excerpt: Arthur Smith has almost recovered from his accident of two weeks ago.

events.title: George Porter returns from Chicago
events.summary: Geo. Porter returned to Medora from Chicago; his wife was expected in about ten days.
events.excerpt: Geo. Porter returned from Chicago last Friday night.

events.title: Theodore Roosevelt arrives and heads to the Elkhorn
events.summary: Theodore Roosevelt came in on Friday night and started almost immediately for his Elkhorn ranch down the river.
events.excerpt: Theodore Roosevelt came in last Friday night and started almost immediatily for his Elkhorn ranch down the river.

events.title: Wal. Osterhout goes to Miles City to buy horses for Howard Eaton
events.summary: Wal. Osterhout went to Miles City to arrange for horses for Howard "Faton" (probably a misprint for Eaton), who followed Monday night.
events.excerpt: Wal. Osterhout went to Miles, Sunday evening to arrange for some horses for Howard Faton

events.title: Former Cow Boy compositor "Sadie" Houk passes through
events.summary: "Sadie" Houk, a Cow Boy compositor the previous summer, passed through Medora on his way to Glendive.
events.excerpt: "Sadie" Houk, who will be remembered as a Cow Boy comp. last summer

events.title: J. D. Garver returns with family from Bismarck
events.summary: Hardware dealer J. D. Garver returned from Bismarck with his family and sister-in-law; his wife's health was improved but she was far from well.
events.excerpt: J. D. Garver returned from Bismarck last Friday, with his family.

events.title: Body of Garfield's niece brought through Medora by stage
events.summary: The body of Mrs. Hawkins of Spearfish, a niece of President Garfield, came up on the stage coach from Spearfish and was shipped from Medora to Mrs. Garfield at Cleveland, Ohio.
events.excerpt: The body of Mrs. Hawkins, of Spearfish, President Garfield's niece, was brought up on the coach Saturday night

events.date_basis: Undated item; defaulted to week before Thu 23 Apr 1885
events.title: Former N. P. superintendent Matthias heads Florida railroad
events.summary: B. F. Matthias, formerly superintendent of the Northern Pacific division through Medora, was reported president of the Charlotte Harbor and Northern Central railroad at Tampa, Florida.
events.excerpt: B. F. Matthias, formerly superintendent of this division of the N. P.

events.title: T. Martin to publish six-month weather digest
events.summary: Mr. T. Martin was to compile a digest of his weather reports for the past six months, to be published with his monthly reports.
events.excerpt: Mr. T. Martin will make a complete digest of his weather reports for the last six months

events.title: Stage driver "Skinny" Wallace paints the town
events.summary: "Skinny" Wallace, a driver on the stage line from Buffalo creek to Middle Grand river, was in town and, the paper joked, "spread a thin coat over the suburbs."
events.excerpt: While here he laid in a good supply of paint and spread a thin coat over the suburbs.

events.title: Rev. H. B. Schaffner preaches at the rink; weekly services begin
events.summary: Rev. H. B. Schaffner preached in the rink to a small congregation kept down by stormy weather; services were to be held every Sunday evening thereafter at 7:30.
events.excerpt: Service will be held every Sunday evening hereafter, at half-past seven.

events.date_basis: "Monday morning" and "Tuesday morning" before Thu 23 Apr 1885
events.title: Lloyd Roberts delivers cattle at Glendive, leaves for St. Cloud
events.summary: Lloyd Roberts returned from Glendive, where he delivered several hundred cattle in prime condition, and left for St. Cloud the next morning; he had also delivered mixed herds at Jamestown and Bismarck.
events.excerpt: He delivered several hundred cattle in Glendive in prime condition.

events.date_basis: Acknowledgment undated; defaulted to week before Thu 23 Apr 1885
events.title: Herd law repealed, fence law set for western Dakota counties
events.summary: The Cow Boy thanked A. McCall of the Black Hills for a list of bills passed by the territorial legislature, noting he originated the bill repealing the herd law and establishing the fence law in the western tier of counties.
events.excerpt: had the bill passed repealing the herd law and establishing the fence law in the western tier of counties

events.title: Eaton family arrives for the summer
events.summary: Mr. and Mrs. Eaton and Miss Hattie Eaton, parents and sister of the Eaton boys, arrived to make their summer headquarters at the logging camp.
events.excerpt: for the summer will make their headquarters at the logging camp

events.title: Falling rock derails engine near Sully Springs
events.summary: The westbound No. 1 was delayed seven or eight hours when it struck a huge rock that had fallen on the track just east of Sully Springs, throwing the engine's front drivers off the track.
events.excerpt: No. 1 was delayed seven or eight hours by the falling of a huge rock upon the track just east of Sully Springs.

events.date_basis: Brand ad in Thu 23 Apr 1885 issue
events.title: Chimney Butte Ranch brand advertised: Theodore Roosevelt, proprietor
events.summary: The Cow Boy carried the brand notice of the Chimney Butte Ranch, Theodore Roosevelt proprietor, with Ferris & Merrifield as managers, ranging six miles south of the railroad on the Little Missouri.
events.excerpt: Chimney Butte Ranch. Theodore Roosevelt, Proprietor. Ferris & Merrifield, Managers.
